critic.argument: The claim 'LLMs can now identify public figures in images' rests on a single low-engagement RSS item whose only content is a bare assertion of a provider differential (Gemini yes, ChatGPT and Claude no). There is no benchmark, no dated test protocol, no screenshot or reproduced prompt, no methodology, and no independent replication. This is self-report/anecdote, not evidence. Worse, the claim as phrased is ambiguous and almost certainly overgeneralized: it conflates 'recognition capability' (the model knows who the person is) with 'provider policy compliance' (the developer chooses to suppress or allow an identity answer). A refusal to name a public figure is a product/policy decision, not proof of an underlying capability differential—so the inference from 'ChatGPT declines' to 'ChatGPT cannot' is a non sequitur. The claim is also time-brittle: model behavior and provider policies change weekly, and an undated assertion cannot support a present-tense 'now' claim. There is additionally a possible lexical slippage in 'identify'—recognizing a face, matching to a known person, and stating a name in output are distinct operations; the source does not disambiguate. Finally, the cluster is a topical mismatch with the stated brief (coding agents, technical leadership, teaching, software craft), suggesting it was scraped by keyword rather than surfaced for relevance, which further erodes its evidentiary standing. The only survivable residue is the narrow, weak reading that some providers appear to allow public-figure identification in image inputs while others do not at some unstated time—a policy snapshot, not a capability finding.
